claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are the most potent producer of type I interferon (IFN).
source: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are the most potent producer of type I interferon (IFN), but how pDC is primed in vivo is poorly defined.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of pDCs cited in the introduction with references (Cella et al., 1999; Siegal et al., 1999; Asselin-Paturel et al., 2001).

claim: CD169+ macrophages prime pDC to initiate type I IFN secretion in the bone marrow of malaria-infected mice.
source: Using a mouse model of severe malaria, we have previously established that upon priming by CD169+ macrophages (MPs), pDC initiates type I IFN-I secretion in the bone marrow (BM) of infected mice via cell-intrinsic TLR7 sensing and cell-extrinsic STING sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work from the authors (Spaulding et al., 2016) as referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: pDC initiation of type I IFN in malaria-infected mice requires cell-intrinsic TLR7 sensing.
source: Using a mouse model of severe malaria, we have previously established that upon priming by CD169+ macrophages (MPs), pDC initiates type I IFN-I secretion in the bone marrow (BM) of infected mice via cell-intrinsic TLR7 sensing and cell-extrinsic STING sensing.
evidence: This is established from previous work (Spaulding et al., 2016) and confirmed with data in the current manuscript showing TLR7-deficient pDCs fail to arrest and produce type I IFN.

claim: pDC initiation of type I IFN in malaria-infected mice requires cell-extrinsic STING sensing.
source: Using a mouse model of severe malaria, we have previously established that upon priming by CD169+ macrophages (MPs), pDC initiates type I IFN-I secretion in the bone marrow (BM) of infected mice via cell-intrinsic TLR7 sensing and cell-extrinsic STING sensing.
evidence: This is established from previous work (Spaulding et al., 2016) and confirmed with data showing STING-deficient CD169+ MPs fail to fully activate pDCs.

claim: CD169+ MP and TLR7 sensing are both required for pDC arrest during priming.
source: Herein we show that CD169+ MP and TLR7 sensing are both required for pDC arrest during priming, suggesting CD169+ MP are the source of TLR7 ligands.
evidence: This is demonstrated through IVM experiments showing pDCs fail to arrest in CD169+ MP-depleted mice and in TLR7-deficient mice (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: CD169+ MP are the source of TLR7 ligands for pDC activation.
source: Herein we show that CD169+ MP and TLR7 sensing are both required for pDC arrest during priming, suggesting CD169+ MP are the source of TLR7 ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both CD169+ MPs and TLR7 are required for pDC arrest, and CD169+ MPs take up Py-iRBCs.

claim: TLR7 sensing in pDC and chemotaxis are both required for pDC arrest and functional communication with CD169+ MP in the BM.
source: We establish that TLR7 sensing in pDC and chemotaxis are both required for pDC arrest and functional communication with CD169+ MP in the BM.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with TLR7-deficient mice and pertussis toxin treatment blocking chemotaxis (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: STING sensing in CD169+ MP controls pDC initiation of type I IFN production.
source: Lastly, we demonstrate that STING sensing in CD169+ MP control pDC initiation of type I IFN production while also regulating pDC clustering and retention/egress from the BM.
evidence: This is demonstrated using conditional knockout mice where STING is deleted specifically in CD169+ MPs (Figure 6).

claim: STING sensing in CD169+ MP regulates pDC clustering and retention/egress from the BM.
source: Lastly, we demonstrate that STING sensing in CD169+ MP control pDC initiation of type I IFN production while also regulating pDC clustering and retention/egress from the BM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by larger pDC clusters and increased pDC numbers in the BM of STING-deficient mice (Figure 5).

claim: pDCs can rapidly secrete up to 1000 times more type I interferon than any other cell.
source: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) (Colonna et al., 2004; Liu, 2005; Reizis, 2019) are equipped with the unique ability to rapidly secrete up to 1000 times more type I interferon (IFN) – both IFNα and IFNβ – than any other cell (Cella et al., 1999; Siegal et al., 1999; Asselin-Paturel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature (Cella et al., 1999; Siegal et al., 1999; Asselin-Paturel et al., 2001).

claim: pDCs constitutively express endosomal Toll-like receptors 7 and 9.
source: pDC-intrinsic features include the constitutive expression of the endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-) 7 and 9, which, respectively, recognize single stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA, leading to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription, the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of their type I IFN producing capacity (Honda et al., 2005b; Honda et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honda et al., 2005a and 2005b, representing established knowledge about pDC biology.

claim: TLR7 recognizes single stranded RNA.
source: pDC-intrinsic features include the constitutive expression of the endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-) 7 and 9, which, respectively, recognize single stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA, leading to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription, the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of their type I IFN producing capacity (Honda et al., 2005b; Honda et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology, supported by citations.

claim: TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA.
source: pDC-intrinsic features include the constitutive expression of the endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-) 7 and 9, which, respectively, recognize single stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA, leading to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription, the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of their type I IFN producing capacity (Honda et al., 2005b; Honda et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology, supported by citations.

claim: TLR7 and TLR9 signaling leads to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription.
source: pDC-intrinsic features include the constitutive expression of the endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-) 7 and 9, which, respectively, recognize single stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA, leading to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription, the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of their type I IFN producing capacity (Honda et al., 2005b; Honda et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honda et al., 2005a and 2005b.

claim: IRF7 is the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of pDC type I IFN producing capacity.
source: pDC-intrinsic features include the constitutive expression of the endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR-) 7 and 9, which, respectively, recognize single stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG motifs containing DNA, leading to type I IFN production via MyD88 signaling and IRF7-mediated transcription, the constitutively highly expressed master regulator of their type I IFN producing capacity (Honda et al., 2005b; Honda et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honda et al., 2005a and 2005b.

claim: Type I IFN modulates hundreds of genes.
source: Type I IFN is a potent immunoregulatory cytokine that modulates hundreds of genes (Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006; Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014; Barrat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006; Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014; Barrat et al., 2019).

claim: Type I IFN promotes early innate immune responses by favoring cell-autonomous defense mechanisms that rapidly restrict viral escape and growth.
source: It promotes early innate immune responses by favoring cell-autonomous defense mechanisms that rapidly restrict viral escape and growth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN function in antiviral immunity.

claim: Type I IFN signaling induces the production of proinflammatory cytokines that enable the mobilization of innate immune defenses.
source: Type I IFN signaling induces the production of proinflammatory cytokines that enable the mobilization of innate immune defenses and set the stage for adaptive immune responses by enhancing antigen processing, presenting, and costimulatory capacities of antigen presenting cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN function.

claim: Type I IFN enhances antigen processing, presenting, and costimulatory capacities of antigen presenting cells.
source: Type I IFN signaling induces the production of proinflammatory cytokines that enable the mobilization of innate immune defenses and set the stage for adaptive immune responses by enhancing antigen processing, presenting, and costimulatory capacities of antigen presenting cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN function.

claim: Type I IFN directly signals to activated T and B cells, promoting expression of anti-apoptotic molecules.
source: It also directly signals to activated T and B cells, promoting expression of anti-apoptotic molecules and orchestrating their differentiation into robust effector cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN function in adaptive immunity.

claim: Type I IFN orchestrates T and B cell differentiation into robust effector cells.
source: It also directly signals to activated T and B cells, promoting expression of anti-apoptotic molecules and orchestrating their differentiation into robust effector cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN function in adaptive immunity.

claim: Excess or dysregulated type I IFN production can promote pathology in auto-immune diseases.
source: In contrast to these beneficial effects, excess or dysregulated type I IFN production that occurs in the context of auto-immune diseases, suggests that type I IFN can also promote pathology (Barrat and Su, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barrat and Su, 2019.

claim: Type I IFN is generally an absolute requirement for effective antiviral immune responses in viral infections.
source: While in viral infections, type I IFN generally appears as an absolute requirement for effective antiviral immune responses, in bacterial (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Listeria monocytogenes) and parasitic (Plasmodium) infections, type I IFN can favor deleterious outcomes (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Spaulding et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2011; Donovan et al., 2017; Mooney et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the contrast with bacterial and parasitic infections where type I IFN can be detrimental.

claim: Type I IFN can favor deleterious outcomes in bacterial infections with Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Listeria monocytogenes.
source: While in viral infections, type I IFN generally appears as an absolute requirement for effective antiviral immune responses, in bacterial (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Listeria monocytogenes) and parasitic (Plasmodium) infections, type I IFN can favor deleterious outcomes (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Spaulding et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2011; Donovan et al., 2017; Mooney et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Spaulding et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2011; Donovan et al., 2017; Mooney et al., 2017).

claim: Type I IFN can favor deleterious outcomes in parasitic Plasmodium infections.
source: While in viral infections, type I IFN generally appears as an absolute requirement for effective antiviral immune responses, in bacterial (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Listeria monocytogenes) and parasitic (Plasmodium) infections, type I IFN can favor deleterious outcomes (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Spaulding et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2011; Donovan et al., 2017; Mooney et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Spaulding et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2011; Donovan et al., 2017; Mooney et al., 2017).

claim: Detrimental type I IFN effects in bacterial and parasitic infections are associated with production of an inappropriate set of inflammatory mediators that hampers or skews the development of an effective host response.
source: This is often associated with the production of an inappropriate set of inflammatory mediators that hampers or skews the development of an effective host response and promotes damaging inflammation, as also exemplified during SARS-CoV-2 infection (Tay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tay et al., 2020 regarding SARS-CoV-2.

claim: pDC-derived type I IFN is essential for host resistance against a range of viral infections.
source: Consistent with the described roles of type I IFN, pDC-derived type I IFN has been reported to be essential for host resistance against a range of viral infections (Reizis, 2019; Barrat and Su, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reizis, 2019 and Barrat and Su, 2019.

claim: pDC-derived type I IFN augments antiviral defense through rapid activation of NK cells, monocytes, and neutrophils.
source: It augments antiviral defense through the rapid activation of innate immune effector responses such as that of NK cells, monocytes, and neutrophils (Cervantes-Barragan et al., 2012; Cervantes-Barragan et al., 2007; Swiecki et al., 2013; Webster et al., 2018; Davidson et al., 2011; Lynch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cervantes-Barragan et al., 2012; Cervantes-Barragan et al., 2007; Swiecki et al., 2013; Webster et al., 2018; Davidson et al., 2011; Lynch et al., 2018).

claim: pDC-derived type I IFN modulates long-term CD8+ and CD4+ T cell survival and differentiation.
source: It also modulates long-term CD8+ and CD4+ T cell survival and differentiation (Swiecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swiecki et al., 2010.

claim: pDC-derived type I IFN promotes autoimmunity in SLE, dermatitis, systemic sclerosis, and type I diabetes.
source: pDC-derived type I IFN also promotes autoimmunity in SLE and dermatitis, systemic sclerosis, and type I diabetes (Barrat and Su, 2019; Hansen et al., 2015; Ah Kioon et al., 2018; Guiducci et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Barrat and Su, 2019; Hansen et al., 2015; Ah Kioon et al., 2018; Guiducci et al., 2010).

claim: In a mouse model of severe lethal malaria, pDC-derived type I IFN drives innate immune cell activation and robust inflammatory responses.
source: Similarly, in a mouse model of severe lethal malaria, pDC-derived type I IFN can drive innate immune cell activation and robust inflammatory responses (Spaulding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spaulding et al., 2016.

claim: pDCs can initiate type I IFN production through direct infection by viruses and TLR7/9 sensing of viral nucleic acids.
source: These include TLR7/9 pDC-intrinsic sensing of viral nucleic acids occurring as a result of direct pDC infection by viruses (Lee et al., 2007; Décembre et al., 2014; Macal et al., 2012; Hornung et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Lee et al., 2007; Décembre et al., 2014; Macal et al., 2012; Hornung et al., 2004).

claim: pDCs can sense pathogen-derived materials from non-pDC-infected cells via exosomes, shedding of immature virus-containing particles, or internalization of immune complexes.
source: Indirect sensing of pathogen-derived materials from non-pDC-infected cells also occurs via exosomes, shedding of immature virus-containing particles or even internalization of immune complexes (Webster et al., 2016; Webster et al., 2018; Décembre et al., 2014; Dreux et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2010; Björck et al., 2008; Rönnblom and Alm, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Webster et al., 2016; Webster et al., 2018; Décembre et al., 2014; Dreux et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2010; Björck et al., 2008; Rönnblom and Alm, 2001).

claim: pDCs form rapid clusters upon TLR7/9-mediated activation.
source: In line with this concept, several studies have reported that pDC forms rapid clusters upon TLR7/9-mediated activation (Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005; Mittelbrunn et al., 2009; Brewitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005; Mittelbrunn et al., 2009; Brewitz et al., 2017).

claim: Systemic injection of synthetic TLR7/9 ligands or murine CMV infection induces pDC to migrate via CXCR3 and CCR7 to the marginal zone of spleens where they achieve peak production of type I IFN.
source: Systemic injection of synthetic TLR7/9 ligands or murine CMV infection induces pDC to migrate via CXCR3 and CCR7 to the marginal zone of spleens where they achieve peak production of type I IFN (Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005.

claim: pDCs can form stable immunological synapses with CD4+ T cells in vitro and upon TLR9-induced activation in the marginal zone/red pulp area.
source: pDC can also form stable immunological synapses with CD4+ T cells in vitro and upon TLR9-induced activation in the marginal zone/red pulp area (Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asselin-Paturel et al., 2005.

claim: During viral infection, lymph node pDCs are recruited via CXCR3 or CCR5 by infected subcapsular CD169+ MP or activated CD8+ T cells to the site of priming and interaction with XCR1+ DC.
source: More recently, lymph node (LN) pDC behavior monitored during viral infection showed that they were recruited via CXCR3 or CCR5, respectively, by infected subcapsular CD169+ MP or activated CD8+ T cells to the site of priming and interaction with XCR1+ DC (Brewitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brewitz et al., 2017.

claim: Type I IFN from pDC promotes local macrophage antiviral response preventing virus spreading and more efficient antigen cross-presentation by DC to CD8+ T cells.
source: Here, type I IFN from pDC promoted (i) local macrophage (MP)-antiviral response preventing virus spreading and more efficient antigen cross-presentation by DC to CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is based on findings from Brewitz et al., 2017 as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: A dynamic TLR7-dependent interferogenic synapse forms between pDC and virus-infected cells in which viral RNA and type I IFN are exchanged.
source: Consistent with these findings, the formation of a dynamic TLR7-dependent interferogenic synapse between pDC- and virus-infected cells was also described in vitro, in which viral RNA and type I IFN were exchanged as possible mechanisms potentiating pDC scanning of infected cells while providing local and targeted delivery of type I IFN (Assil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Assil et al., 2019.

claim: Tissue trafficking and localization of pDC in situ is essential for them to undergo activation and for their optimal function.
source: These results therefore suggested that tissue trafficking and localization of pDC in situ is essential for them to undergo activation and for their optimal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the studies on pDC clustering, migration, and interactions with other cells described in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: pDC arrested in the BM of Py-infected mice at the time of peak type I IFN production (~1.5 days).
source: We have previously established that (1) CD169+ MP prime pDC to initiate rapid type I IFN production in the bone marrow (BM) of mice infected with lethal Plasmodium yoelii (Py) YM (Spaulding et al., 2016), (2) pDC priming involved pDC-intrinsic TLR7 and pDC-extrinsic STING sensing, and (3) pDC arrested in the BM of infected mice at the time of peak type I IFN production (~1.5 days) using intravital microscopy (IVM) while they were highly motile in the BM of naive mice.
evidence: This is from previous work by the authors (Spaulding et al., 2016).

claim: pDCs are highly motile in the BM of naive mice.
source: We have previously established that (1) CD169+ MP prime pDC to initiate rapid type I IFN production in the bone marrow (BM) of mice infected with lethal Plasmodium yoelii (Py) YM (Spaulding et al., 2016), (2) pDC priming involved pDC-intrinsic TLR7 and pDC-extrinsic STING sensing, and (3) pDC arrested in the BM of infected mice at the time of peak type I IFN production (~1.5 days) using intravital microscopy (IVM) while they were highly motile in the BM of naive mice.
evidence: This is from previous work by the authors and confirmed in the current manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: pDC arrested near or potentially in contact with CD169+ MP in Py-infected BM.
source: pDC arrested near or potentially in contact with CD169+ MP, however, these MPs were also densely distributed throughout the BM making it difficult to establish a functional interaction.
evidence: This is from previous observations that motivated the current study.

claim: CD169+ MP are tissue-resident MP which localize at entry ports of lymphatics in dLNs and in splenic marginal zones.
source: CD169+ MP are tissue-resident MP, which localizes at entry ports of lymphatics in dLNs and in splenic marginal zones.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD169+ macrophages.

claim: CD169+ MP capture and sample antigens from dead cells.
source: They capture and sample antigens from dead cells, and act as entry points for viruses and bacteria, subsequently initiating immune defenses (Sung et al., 2012; Kastenmüller et al., 2012; Perez et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Sung et al., 2012; Kastenmüller et al., 2012; Perez et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2007).

claim: CD169+ MP act as entry points for viruses and bacteria, subsequently initiating immune defenses.
source: They capture and sample antigens from dead cells, and act as entry points for viruses and bacteria, subsequently initiating immune defenses (Sung et al., 2012; Kastenmüller et al., 2012; Perez et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Sung et al., 2012; Kastenmüller et al., 2012; Perez et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2007).

claim: Two subpopulations of CD169+ MP exist in the BM, defined as F4/80hi CD169int and F4/80int CD169hi.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed the presence of two subpopulations of CD169+ MP in the BM, which we defined phenotypically as F4/80hi CD169int (F4/80hi MP subset) and F4/80int CD169hi (CD169hi MP subset) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both F4/80hi and CD169hi BM MP took up significantly increased proportions of Py-infected iRBCs compared to uRBCs, with a ~10-fold higher uptake.
source: As early as 6 hr post-transfer of TAMRA-Red+ RBC, both F4/80hi and CD169hi BM MP took up significantly increased proportions of Py-infected iRBCs compared to uRBCs, with a ~10-fold higher uptake of infected relative to uninfected RBC in both CD169+ MP subsets (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: pDCs do not directly take up Py-iRBCs.
source: Of note, we did not detect direct uptake of Py-iRBCs by pDC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In vivo labeling of CD169+ MP with anti-CD169 mAb does not interfere with Py-iRBC uptake.
source: Py-iRBC uptake was also comparable in mice injected with anti-CD169 mAb or control isotype Ab prior to the transfer of TAMRA-Red+ iRBC, ruling out that the in vivo labeling of CD169+ MP interfered with Py-iRBC uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Time-lapse IVM imaging confirmed Py-iRBC attachment and accumulation on CD169+ MP in the BM.
source: Time-lapse IVM imaging confirmed Py-iRBC attachment and accumulation on CD169+ MP in the BM, and possibly internalization (Figure 1B and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM imaging shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Both populations of CD169+ MP take up Py-iRBC in the BM of infected mice in vivo.
source: Thus, taken together these data show that both populations of CD169+ MP take up Py-iRBC in the BM of infected mice in vivo, consistent with the hypothesis that MP can present parasite-derived materials and provide activating signals to pDC.
evidence: This is concluded from the FACS and IVM data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CD169+ MP can present parasite-derived materials and provide activating signals to pDC.
source: Thus, taken together these data show that both populations of CD169+ MP take up Py-iRBC in the BM of infected mice in vivo, consistent with the hypothesis that MP can present parasite-derived materials and provide activating signals to pDC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD169+ MPs take up Py-iRBCs and are required for pDC activation.

claim: There is a significant loss (>50%) of both CD169hi and F4/80hi MP subsets in the BM of Py-infected mice between 30 and 36 hr post-infection.
source: We found a significant loss (>50%) of both MP subsets in the BM of Py-infected mice, that occurred between 30 and 36 hr post-infection as quantified by FACS analysis (Figure 1C) and IVM imaging of the tibial BM where the decrease in the overall BM MP numbers was also visualized in situ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis (Figure 1C) and IVM imaging (Figure 1D).

claim: Sca-1, CD80, and ICAM-1 expression are increased on CD169+ MP in response to Py infection.
source: In addition, Sca-1, CD80 costimulatory molecule, and ICAM-1 integrin ligand expression were increased while CD11a was diminished, consistent with robust activation of both subsets of MP in response to Py infection (Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD11a expression is diminished on CD169+ MP in response to Py infection.
source: In addition, Sca-1, CD80 costimulatory molecule, and ICAM-1 integrin ligand expression were increased while CD11a was diminished, consistent with robust activation of both subsets of MP in response to Py infection (Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD169+ MP in the BM of Py-infected mice undergo robust activation.
source: In addition, Sca-1, CD80 costimulatory molecule, and ICAM-1 integrin ligand expression were increased while CD11a was diminished, consistent with robust activation of both subsets of MP in response to Py infection (Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by changes in activation marker expression shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In uninfected WT mice, pDCs are motile with a track velocity of 7.14 μm/min.
source: In WT uninfected mice, pDC was motile, exhibiting long tracks and a TV of 7.14 μm/min (Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—video 1), faster than their reported speed of 5 μm/min in LNs (Mittelbrunn et al., 2009), but slower than naive T cells in the LN that travel at 10–15 μm/min (Shigematsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: pDCs in uninfected BM migrate through and explore a large volume of parenchymal tissue (~1350 μm2/hr).
source: Based on their DR (1.5 μm/min) and MSD, pDC migrated through and explored a large volume of parenchymal tissue (~1350 μm2/hr), similar to LN lymphocytes (Mittelbrunn et al., 2009) and consistent with a scanning role in the BM (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is calculated from IVM data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: CD169+ MP are sessile in both naive and infected mice.
source: In contrast, CD169+ MP were sessile, whether in naive or infected mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MSD analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After Py infection, pDC track velocity is reduced to 5.13 μm/min.
source: After Py infection, pDC tracks, TV (5.13 μm/min), DR (0.93 μm/min), and MSD were all significantly reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: After Py infection, pDC displacement rate is reduced to 0.93 μm/min.
source: After Py infection, pDC tracks, TV (5.13 μm/min), DR (0.93 μm/min), and MSD were all significantly reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Diphtheria toxin injection in siglec1DTR mice induces selective depletion of both subsets of CD169+ MP.
source: In siglec1DTR mice, whether chimeric or not, diphtheria toxin (DT) injection induced the selective depletion of both subsets of CD169+ MP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In Py-infected, DT-treated mice, pDC displacement rate and MSD are significantly increased compared to untreated mice.
source: Interestingly, IVM imaging of Py-infected DT-treated mice revealed much longer pDC tracks compared to untreated control mice (Figure 2E). Moreover, pDC DR and MSD were significantly increased compared to untreated mice (by ~50%, Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 2E, F, G and Figure 2—video 2.

claim: CD169+ MP control pDC dynamics during Py infection.
source: Thus, these data collectively establish that CD169+ MP control pDC dynamics during Py infection and suggest that pDC arrest is linked to their ability to initiate type I IFN production.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that depletion of CD169+ MPs prevents pDC arrest.

claim: pDC arrest is linked to their ability to initiate type I IFN production.
source: Thus, these data collectively establish that CD169+ MP control pDC dynamics during Py infection and suggest that pDC arrest is linked to their ability to initiate type I IFN production.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that conditions preventing pDC arrest also prevent type I IFN production.

claim: In both Tlr7−/y and WT uninfected mice, pDCs are highly motile with comparable track velocities (6.52 and 7.16 μm/min respectively).
source: In both Tlr7−/y and WT uninfected mice, pDC was highly motile with long tracks and a comparable TV (respectively, 6.52 and 7.16 μm/min, Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: pDCs in Tlr7−/y uninfected mice exhibit greater motility than WT, suggesting tonic TLR7 signals regulate pDC motility under steady-state conditions.
source: Interestingly, pDC in Tlr7−/y uninfected mice exhibit greater motility, suggesting that tonic TLR7 signals regulate pDC motility under steady-state conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pDC motility in WT versus Tlr7−/y uninfected mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Following Py infection in WT mice, pDC motility is reduced by 31% in terms of track velocity and 45% based on displacement rate.
source: Following Py infection in WT mice, pDC motility was reduced by 31%, in terms of TV (4.92 μm/min) and 45% based on DR (~0.87 μm/min), as well as for MSD and slope of MSD averages (Figure 3B, D and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 3B, D and Figure 3—video 2.

claim: pDCs in Py-infected Tlr7−/y mice do not arrest and continue migrating with similar speeds as uninfected mice.
source: In contrast, pDC in Py-infected Tlr7−/y mice did not arrest and continued migrating with similar speeds in terms of TV (7.05 μm/min) and DR (1.55 μm/min, Figure 3B, C) despite detectable measurable MSD reductions (Figure 3D) reflecting a more restricted migration pattern, but not arrest.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 3B, C, D.

claim: Tlr7−/y pDCs in infected chimeras exhibit long tracks and do not arrest while WT pDCs arrest.
source: Consistent with the prior result (Figure 3A–D), Tlr7−/y pDC in infected chimeras exhibited long tracks and did not arrest while WT pDC had much shorter tracks and arrested, establishing that TLR7 signaling intrinsic to pDC, is required for them to stop during infection (Figure 3E, F and Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis of chimeric mice shown in Figure 3E, F and Figure 3—video 3.

claim: TLR7 signaling intrinsic to pDC is required for pDCs to arrest during infection.
source: Consistent with the prior result (Figure 3A–D), Tlr7−/y pDC in infected chimeras exhibited long tracks and did not arrest while WT pDC had much shorter tracks and arrested, establishing that TLR7 signaling intrinsic to pDC, is required for them to stop during infection (Figure 3E, F and Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis of chimeric mice shown in Figure 3E, F and Figure 3—video 3.

claim: WT pDCs significantly increase their contact times with CD169+ MPs during infection (from ~2 to 16 min).
source: We also quantified pDC/CD169+ MP contact durations using a Kiss and Run algorithm (Imaris) as a measure of their possible interactions in chimeric mice and found that WT pDC significantly increased their contact times with the MP during infection (from ~2 to 16 min) whereas Tlr7−/y pDC interacted with the MP for comparable amounts of time (~4–5 min) whether mice were infected or not (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by contact duration analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Tlr7−/y pDCs interact with CD169+ MPs for comparable amounts of time (~4–5 min) whether mice are infected or not.
source: We also quantified pDC/CD169+ MP contact durations using a Kiss and Run algorithm (Imaris) as a measure of their possible interactions in chimeric mice and found that WT pDC significantly increased their contact times with the MP during infection (from ~2 to 16 min) whereas Tlr7−/y pDC interacted with the MP for comparable amounts of time (~4–5 min) whether mice were infected or not (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by contact duration analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TLR7 sensing in pDC is required for their arrest and potential interactions with CD169+ MP in the BM of malaria-infected mice.
source: Thus, taken together, these results show that TLR7 sensing in pDC is required for their arrest and potential interactions with CD169+ MP in the BM of malaria-infected mice at the time pDC produce peak type I IFN.
evidence: This is concluded from the IVM and contact duration data in Figure 3.

claim: CD169+ MPs are providing TLR7 ligands to pDCs.
source: Since CD169+ MP are required for pDC arrest, it further suggests that MP are providing TLR7 ligands to pDC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both CD169+ MPs and TLR7 are required for pDC arrest.

claim: CCR9 and CX3CR1 are significantly upregulated on pDCs after Py infection in WT but not in Tlr7−/y mice.
source: While basal expression of these receptors and integrins was comparable in all groups of uninfected mice, CCR9 and CX3CR1 were significantly upregulated on pDC after infection in WT but not in Tlr7−/y mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CXCR3 expression is significantly downregulated on pDCs in both WT and Tlr7−/y mice after Py infection, but to different extents (90% and 50%, respectively).
source: In contrast, CXCR3 expression was significantly downregulated on pDC in both WT and Tlr7−/y mice, but to different extents (90% and 50%, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ICAM-1 expression is significantly upregulated on pDCs in both WT and Tlr7−/y mice after Py infection, but the magnitude of upregulation is substantially greater in WT mice (factor of ~3).
source: Expression of ICAM-1, a ligand for the integrin LFA-1, was significantly upregulated in both WT and Tlr7−/y after infection, but the magnitude of upregulation remained substantially greater in WT mice (factor of ~3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CD11a expression is slightly decreased on pDCs in Py-infected WT mice whereas expression does not change in Tlr7−/y mice.
source: Expression of CD11a, the alpha chain of LFA-1, was slightly decreased in Py-infected WT mice whereas expression did not change in Tlr7−/y mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VCAM-1 expression is significantly reduced on pDCs in both WT and Tlr7−/y mice during Py infection, but to a lesser extent in Tlr7−/y mice.
source: Lastly, expression of VCAM-1, ligand for the integrin VLA-4, was significantly reduced in both WT and Tlr7−/y during the infection, but to a lesser extent in Tlr7−/y mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TLR7-mediated sensing by pDCs is linked to changes in cell-surface expression of chemotactic receptors and adhesion molecules that may contribute to modifications in pDC motility, homing, and/or arrest following Py infection.
source: Collectively, these data link TLR7-mediated sensing by pDCs to changes in cell-surface expression of several chemotactic receptors and adhesion molecules that may contribute to modifications in pDC motility, homing, and/or arrest that occur following Py infection.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential expression of chemokine receptors and adhesion molecules in WT versus Tlr7−/y mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pertussis toxin treatment leads to stronger immobilization of pDCs in Py-infected mice compared to control mice.
source: In Py-infected PTCRA-EGFP reporter mice, PT treatment led to stronger immobilization of pDC compared to control mice, with shorter tracks and significantly lower DR (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: pDC arrest after pertussis toxin treatment is concomitant with distinct morphological changes to a round shape.
source: pDC arrest was also concomitant with distinct morphological changes (Figure 4C). Notably, pDCs in PT-treated mice exhibited a round shape contrasting with the elongated dendritic shape observed in PBS-treated counterparts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Quantitative analysis reveals significant differences in pDC length, surface, and shape factor in PT- versus PBS-treated Py-infected mice.
source: Quantitative analysis of individual pDC length, surface, and shape factor (a measure of cell sphericity) further revealed significant differences in PT- versus PBS-treated Py-infected mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative morphology analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Pertussis toxin treatment results in an 80% reduction in type I IFN-expressing pDCs compared to control infected group.
source: To determine whether PT treatment impacted the ability of pDC to make type I IFN, we carried out the same experiment in IfnbYFP/YFP reporter mice (Scheu et al., 2008), which revealed an 80% reduction in type I IFN-expressing pDC (YFP+) compared to control infected group (0.44% vs. 2.1% YFP+ pDCs, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis of IfnbYFP/YFP reporter mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GαI-protein-dependent transduction is required to achieve maximal type I IFN production by pDCs.
source: Taken together with the imaging findings, this indicated that GαI-protein-dependent transduction was required to achieve maximal type I IFN production.
evidence: This is concluded from the pertussis toxin experiments showing reduced type I IFN production.

claim: Expression of CD62L, ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and CXCR3 but not CD86 are significantly altered in PT- compared to PBS-treated Py-infected mice.
source: Despite their drastic immobilization and morphological changes, pDC in PT-treated infected mice still modulated cell-surface expression of costimulatory (CD86) and adhesion (CD62L, ICAM-1, VCAM-1) molecules, as well as chemotactic receptors (CXCR3), compared to PBS-treated infected and uninfected control mice (Figure 4E). Specifically, expression of CD62L, ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and CXCR3 but not CD86, were significantly altered in PT- compared to PBS-treated Py-infected mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Blocking GαI-protein-coupled receptor signal transduction including chemotaxis alters expression of most but not all activation markers and the acquisition of type I IFN-secreting capacity by pDCs.
source: These results show that blocking GαI-protein-coupled receptor signal transduction including chemotaxis, alters expression of most but not all of these markers, and the acquisition of type I IFN-secreting capacity by the pDC.
evidence: This is concluded from the pertussis toxin experiments showing differential effects on various markers.

claim: Antibody blocking of CXCR3 and CXCL9 does not decrease type I IFN expression by pDCs.
source: We injected IfnbYFP/YFP mice at the time of infection both with anti-CXCR3 (CXCR3-173 clone) and anti-CXCL9 2A6.9.9 mAb, which blocks the CXCL10-binding site and neutralizes soluble CXCL9, respectively (Figure 4F). pDC in these mice expressed YFP at similar levels relative to control-isotype Ab-treated or non-treated mice (1.5–2%).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Antibody blocking of LFA-1 and VLA-4 integrins, with or without anti-CXCR3 mAb, does not decrease type I IFN expression by pDCs.
source: Furthermore, Ab blocking of LFA-1 and VLA-4 integrins, with or without anti-CXCR3 mAb, also failed to decrease expression of type I IFN by the pDC, suggesting that none of the tested reagents were sufficient to recapitulate the in vivo effects of PT treatment on pDC activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: pDC motility requires GαI-dependent chemotaxis which controls pDC homing to where TLR7 ligands are.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that pDC motility requires GαI-dependent chemotaxis. This process controls pDC homing to where TLR7 ligands are, and direct or indirect functional interactions with CD169+ MP to initiate type I IFN production.
evidence: This is concluded from the pertussis toxin and antibody blocking experiments.

claim: In uninfected Sting1Gt/Gt mice, most pDCs exhibit high motility while they arrest in Py-infected counterparts.
source: To investigate these possibilities, we analyzed pDC motility in Sting1Gt/Gt PTCRA-EGFP reporter mice by IVM. In uninfected Sting1Gt/Gt mice, most pDC exhibited high motility while they arrested in Py-infected counterparts (Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1.

claim: pDC displacement rate and MSD slopes are significantly diminished in Py-infected Sting1Gt/Gt mice compared to naive mice.
source: While pDC DR and MSD slopes were significantly diminished compared to naive mice, the average pDC TV remained elevated (6.52 μm/min), similar to that of uninfected mice (6.33 μm/min) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The MSD of pDCs is significantly higher in Sting1Gt/Gt compared to WT-infected mice.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the MSD of pDC was significantly higher in Sting1Gt/Gt compared to WT-infected mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MSD analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WT pDCs in a Sting1Gt/Gt host arrest and have longer contact durations with MPs compared to control WT chimera mice.
source: In these mice where we visualized WT pDC in a Sting1Gt/Gt host, pDC arrested and had longer contact durations with MP compared to control WT chimera and non-chimera mice (Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM analysis of chimeric mice shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—video 2.

claim: In Py-infected Sting1Gt/Gt mice, pDC clusters are significantly larger in volume than in WT control mice, by threefold on average.
source: Most interestingly, we observed that in both non-chimera Py-infected Sting1Gt/Gt mice, pDC clusters were significantly larger in volume than in WT control mice, by threefold on average, and in some cases exceeding WT clusters by tenfold (Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cluster volume quantification shown in Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—videos 2 and 3.

claim: Higher numbers of pDCs are enumerated in the BM of Sting1Gt/Gt compared to WT IfnbYFP/YFP reporter Py-infected mice.
source: We also enumerated by FACS analysis higher numbers of pDC in the BM of Sting1Gt/Gt compared to WT IfnbYFP/YFP reporter Py-infected mice (Figure 5I), correlating with the significantly larger clusters of pDC quantified in the BM of Sting1Gt/Gt mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The number of Ifnb-expressing pDCs (YFP+) is significantly reduced in Sting1Gt/Gt mice compared to WT counterparts, despite increased pDC numbers.
source: As expected, the number of Ifnb-expressing pDC (YFP+) was significantly reduced compared to WT counterparts, despite increased pDC numbers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Expression of chemotactic receptors (CXCR3, CCR9, CXCR4, CX3CR1) and the integrin VCAM-1 fail to undergo as much cell-surface modulation in Sting1Gt/Gt mice as in WT mice.
source: In addition, while still significantly modulated, expression of several chemotactic receptors (CXCR3, CCR9, CXCR4, CX3CR1) and the integrin VCAM-1, failed to undergo as much cell-surface modulation as in WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: pDCs in Sting1Gt/Gt mice may not receive appropriate signals to enable them to resume motility, leave clusters and egress from the BM.
source: This suggested that pDC in Sting1Gt/Gt mice may not receive appropriate signals to enable them to resume motility, leave clusters and egress from the BM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of larger clusters, increased pDC numbers, and altered chemokine receptor expression in Sting1Gt/Gt mice.

claim: pDC-extrinsic, STING-dependent signals do not control pDC homing and arrest in the BM during Py infection.
source: Taken together, these data establish that pDC-extrinsic, STING-dependent signals do not control pDC homing and arrest in the BM during Py infection, but that they may control pDC functional interactions with CD169+ MP and egress from the BM, thereby limiting their accumulation and/or retention in the BM.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that pDCs still arrest in Sting1Gt/Gt mice but accumulate in larger numbers.

claim: STING-dependent signals control pDC functional interactions with CD169+ MP and egress from the BM.
source: Taken together, these data establish that pDC-extrinsic, STING-dependent signals do not control pDC homing and arrest in the BM during Py infection, but that they may control pDC functional interactions with CD169+ MP and egress from the BM, thereby limiting their accumulation and/or retention in the BM.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of larger pDC clusters and increased pDC numbers in Sting1Gt/Gt mice.

claim: STING signaling in CD169+ MP is required for pDC priming of type I IFN producing capacity, with a ~60% reduction in YFP+ pDCs when STING is lacking in CD169+ MPs.
source: Upon Py YM infection, while ~2.2% of pDC (~4200 pDC/leg) in WT and Sting11Gt/WT control mice expressed IFNβ (YFP+ ICAM-1hi), we quantified a ~60% reduction in YFP+ pDC when STING was lacking in CD169+ MPs (Figure 6A), demonstrating that STING signaling in CD169+ MP was required for pDC priming of type I IFN producing capacity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis of conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In mice where CD169+ MP lack STING, the number of pDCs in BM is ~1.5 times higher than in WT or Sting11Gt/WT control groups.
source: Interestingly, in these mice where CD169+ MP lacked STING, the number of pDC in BM was ~1.5 times higher than in WT or Sting11Gt/WT control groups (p value = 0.1, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Similar increases in numbers of pDCs are enumerated in the BM of whole-body STING-deficient (Sting1Gt/Gt) or CD169+ MP-depleted (DT-treated siglec1DTR/WT) infected mice.
source: Similar increases in numbers of pDC were also enumerated in the BM of whole-body STING-deficient (Sting1Gt/Gt) or CD169+ MP-depleted (DT-treated siglec1DTR/WT) infected mice, consistent with retention of pDC in BM when CD169+ MP or STING-dependent signals were absent (Figure 5G–I and Figure 5—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5G–I and Figure 5—videos 2 and 3.

claim: STING signaling in CD169+ MP during Py infection provides pDCs with key signal(s) to initiate type I IFN production and egress from the BM.
source: Collectively, these results show that STING signaling in CD169+ MP during Py infection, provide pDC with key signal(s) to initiate type I IFN production and egress from the BM.
evidence: This is concluded from the conditional knockout experiments showing reduced type I IFN production and increased pDC retention when STING is absent in CD169+ MPs.

claim: In whole-body Sting1Gt/Gt mice, CD169hi but not F4/80hi MP are partially protected from loss compared to WT control mice (by ~50%).
source: In whole-body Sting1Gt/Gt mice, CD169hi but not F4/80hi MP, were partially protected from loss compared to WT control mice (by ~50%, Figure 6C), suggesting that this may prevent optimal pDC priming.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice where STING is selectively lacking in CD169+ MP, both MP populations undergo similar loss as in WT mice.
source: However, in siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice where STING is selectively lacking in CD169+ MP, both MP populations underwent similar loss as in WT mice, suggesting STING deficiency extrinsic to MP, protects CD169hi MP from loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: STING deficiency extrinsic to MP protects CD169hi MP from loss.
source: However, in siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice where STING is selectively lacking in CD169+ MP, both MP populations underwent similar loss as in WT mice, suggesting STING deficiency extrinsic to MP, protects CD169hi MP from loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of MP loss in whole-body versus conditional STING-deficient mice.

claim: In siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice, pDCs fail to initiate type I IFN transcription and accumulate in the BM compared to control groups.
source: However, in siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice, pDC failed to initiate type I IFN transcription and accumulated in the BM compared to control groups (Figures 5I and 6B), consistent with a model in which STING signaling in CD169+ MP provide activating signals to pDC that are unrelated to their loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5I and 6B.

claim: STING signaling in CD169+ MP provides activating signals to pDCs that are unrelated to MP loss.
source: However, in siglec1Cre/WTSting1Gt/F mice, pDC failed to initiate type I IFN transcription and accumulated in the BM compared to control groups (Figures 5I and 6B), consistent with a model in which STING signaling in CD169+ MP provide activating signals to pDC that are unrelated to their loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pDCs fail to activate even when MP loss is similar to WT.

claim: MP activation 36 hr post-infection, as measured by cell-surface modulation of MHC-II, CD80, ICAM-1, and Sca-1, is mostly comparable in all infected groups.
source: Of note, MP activation 36 hr post-infection, as measured by cell-surface modulation of MHC-II, CD80, ICAM-1, and Sca-1, was mostly comparable in all infected groups, likely ruling out a general activation defect of STING-deficient MP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MP loss during Py infection is uncoupled from STING-mediated priming of pDCs by CD169+ MP.
source: In summary, these data uncouple MP loss that occurs during Py infection from STING-mediated priming of pDC by CD169+ MP.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that pDC activation defects occur independently of MP loss patterns.

claim: A functional interaction (direct or indirect) exists between CD169+ MP and pDC in vivo that is needed to license pDC priming of type I IFN production during malaria infection.
source: Here, we reveal a complex multi-cell choreography that orchestrates pDC production of type I IFN during malaria infection. We establish the existence of a functional interaction (direct or indirect) between CD169+ MP and pDC in vivo that is needed to license pDC priming of type I IFN production in vivo during this infection.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: pDC arrest is linked to their optimal priming.
source: We link pDC arrest to their optimal priming.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing that conditions preventing arrest also prevent optimal type I IFN production.

claim: CD169+ MP take up parasite-infected RBCs in the BM.
source: We show that CD169+ MP take up parasite-infected RBCs in the BM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS and IVM data in Figure 1.

claim: MP-intrinsic STING sensing is required to activate pDC production of type I IFN.
source: We also show that MP-intrinsic STING sensing is required to activate pDC production of type I IFN, and enable their egress/release from the BM after priming (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by conditional knockout experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: MP-intrinsic STING sensing enables pDC egress/release from the BM after priming.
source: We also show that MP-intrinsic STING sensing is required to activate pDC production of type I IFN, and enable their egress/release from the BM after priming (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased pDC retention in the BM when STING is absent in CD169+ MPs.

claim: CD169+ MP in the BM act as first-line responders to infection, akin to other CD169+ MP found in the LN and spleen.
source: These findings are therefore consistent with a model in which CD169+ MP in the BM act as first-line responders to infection, akin to other CD169+ MP found in the LN and spleen (Grabowska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by citation to Grabowska et al., 2018.

claim: Depletion of CD169+ MP prior to infection prevents type I IFN production by pDCs.
source: Depletion of these MP prior to infection prevents type I production by pDCs (Spaulding et al., 2016), indicating that these antigen presenting cells are non-redundant and uniquely capable of providing Py ligands and/or other innate signals to pDC in the BM.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spaulding et al., 2016.

claim: CD169+ MP are non-redundant and uniquely capable of providing Py ligands and/or other innate signals to pDC in the BM.
source: Depletion of these MP prior to infection prevents type I production by pDCs (Spaulding et al., 2016), indicating that these antigen presenting cells are non-redundant and uniquely capable of providing Py ligands and/or other innate signals to pDC in the BM.
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion experiments.

claim: pDC motility, homing and functional interactions with MP are prerequisites to achieve type I IFN production.
source: The fact that depletion of CD169+ MP and cell-intrinsic lack of TLR7 prevent pDC arrest establishes that pDC motility, homing and functional interactions with MP are prerequisites to achieve type I IFN production.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing that preventing arrest also prevents type I IFN production.

claim: TLR7 ligands are not freely diffusing in the BM and/or pDCs require nucleic acids to be properly presented or packaged to access TLR7-containing endosomes in vivo.
source: These results suggest that TLR7 ligands, which trigger pDC arrest and type I production, are also not freely diffusing in the BM and/or that in vivo, pDC require nucleic acids to be properly presented or packaged to access TLR7-containing endosomes in pDC.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both CD169+ MPs and TLR7 for pDC arrest.

claim: Direct or indirect interactions with CD169+ MPs are required to deliver Py-derived ligands to pDCs in the BM.
source: In either case, we propose that direct or indirect interactions with CD169+ MPs are required to deliver Py-derived ligands to pDCs in the BM.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: pDCs sense hepatitis C-infected hepatocytes via viral RNA-containing exosomes.
source: This finding is consistent with prior studies showing pDC sensing of hepatitis C-infected hepatocytes via viral RNA-containing exosomes (Dreux et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2010) or cellular particles containing Dengue virus (Décembre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dreux et al., 2012 and Takahashi et al., 2010.

claim: pDCs are directly infected by specific viruses such as herpes simplex virus and arenaviruses.
source: pDC was also reported to be directly infected by specific viruses such as herpes simplex virus and arenaviruses, and to utilize specialized intracellular processes like autophagy to sense viral nucleic acids and initiate type I IFN production (Lee et al., 2007; Macal et al., 2012; Assil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2007; Macal et al., 2012; Assil et al., 2019.

claim: pDCs utilize autophagy to sense viral nucleic acids and initiate type I IFN production.
source: pDC was also reported to be directly infected by specific viruses such as herpes simplex virus and arenaviruses, and to utilize specialized intracellular processes like autophagy to sense viral nucleic acids and initiate type I IFN production (Lee et al., 2007; Macal et al., 2012; Assil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2007; Macal et al., 2012; Assil et al., 2019.

claim: Given the very low frequency and numbers of pDCs but their rapid response, pDCs are likely using indirect but more effective modes of recognition.
source: Given the very low frequency and numbers of pDC but their rapid response, it is likely that pDC are largely using such indirect but more effective modes of recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the biology of pDCs and their response kinetics.

claim: The formation of specialized cell–cell structures between pDCs and infected cells or cells presenting pathogen-derived molecules mediates both uptake and sensing of TLR ligands and the local delivery of type I IFN in interferogenic synapses.
source: The formation of specialized cell–cell structures between pDC and infected cells or cells presenting pathogen-derived molecules, is indeed proposed to mediate both uptake and sensing of TLR ligands and the local delivery of type I IFN in interferogenic synapses (Assil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Assil et al., 2019.

claim: Proper clustering and arrest of pDCs is a TLR7 guided process.
source: Proper clustering and arrest of pDCs is a TLR7 guided process.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing TLR7 is required for pDC arrest and clustering.

claim: TLR7 is required in pDCs for their arrest, type I IFN production, and extensive remodeling of chemokine receptor and adhesion molecule expression.
source: TLR7 is required in pDC for their arrest, and type I production, as well as extensive remodeling of pDC expression of chemokine receptors and adhesion molecules, likely promoting stable contacts with activated, Py-loaded MPs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with TLR7-deficient mice showing defects in all these processes.

claim: In vivo, pDCs are recruited via CXCR3- and CCR5-dependent chemotaxis to virus-infected subcapsular draining LN MP or CD8+ T cells for local delivery of type I IFN.
source: In vivo, pDC are recruited via CXCR3- and CCR5-dependent chemotaxis to virus-infected subcapsular draining LN MP or CD8+ T cells, respectively, for local delivery of type I IFN, rapidly restricting early virus spreading while promoting effective T cell priming (Brewitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brewitz et al., 2017.

claim: pDC chemotaxis processes are likely to be redundant given that pDCs express multiple chemotactic receptors.
source: Given that pDC expresses multiple chemotactic receptors, and some are significantly up- or downregulated during Py infection (e.g., CCR9, CXCR3, CX3CR1), these processes are likely to be redundant.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of multiple chemokine receptors and the failure of single receptor blockade to prevent activation.

claim: Blockade of CXCR3-mediated chemotaxis fails to recapitulate all GαI-mediated chemotaxis blockade effects.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, blockade of CXCR3-mediated chemotaxis failed to recapitulate all GαI-mediated chemotaxis blockade.
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Co-blockade of several adhesion molecules (LFA-1, VLA-4) does not abrogate the production of type I IFN by pDCs.
source: Even co-blockade of several adhesion molecules (LFA-1, VLA-4) involved in classical leukocyte adhesion and clustering, did not abrogate the production of type I IFN by pDC, suggesting that other chemotactic and adhesion mechanisms are involved and further investigations are needed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: It was unexpected that STING does not control pDC arrest despite controlling full pDC activation and pDC interactions with CD169+ MP.
source: Finally, we establish TLR7-dependent arrest and interaction of pDC with CD169+ MP. We also show that full activation of pDC requires STING signaling in CD169+ MP and that MP control pDC arrest. It was therefore unexpected that we did not find STING controls pDC arrest.
evidence: This reflects the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: In STING-deficient mice, pDCs form significantly greater size clusters and accumulate in higher numbers in the BM compared to WT counterparts.
source: However, we revealed that in STING-deficient mice, pDC formed significantly greater size clusters and accumulated in higher numbers in the BM compared to WT counterparts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IVM and FACS data in Figure 5.

claim: STING-dependent signals control pDC egress from the BM and the organization of pDC clusters.
source: This result was confirmed in mice lacking STING in the radioresistant compartment and only in CD169+ MP, consistent with a model where STING-dependent signals control pDC egress from the BM, and as a consequence, the organization of pDC clusters.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with conditional STING knockout in CD169+ MPs.

claim: pDC numbers in the BM of Py-infected mice decrease after peak type I IFN production while blood pDC numbers increase.
source: In our previous work (Spaulding et al., 2016), we reported that pDC numbers in the BM of Py-infected mice decreased after peak type I IFN production while that of blood pDC increased.
evidence: This is from previous work by the authors (Spaulding et al., 2016).

claim: Larger clusters and increased numbers of pDCs in STING-deficient mice may indicate that pDCs are not fully activating and remain docked, awaiting additional signals.
source: Larger clusters and increased numbers of pDC in STING-deficient mice, and in mice with STING-deficient CD169+ MP, may indicate that pDC are not fully activating and thus remain docked, awaiting for additional signals.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: Large clusters of pDCs are evidence that pDC priming is spatially segregated in the BM and that activation signals are not freely diffusing.
source: These large clusters of pDC are further evidence that pDC priming is spatially segregated in the BM and that activation signals are not freely diffusing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of pDC clustering patterns.

claim: The identity of STING-dependent signal(s) delivered from Py-activated CD169+ MP to pDCs remains unknown.
source: In particular, which STING-dependent signal(s) are delivered from Py-activated CD169+ MP to pDC remains unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: STING was originally identified as a cytosolic nucleic-acid sensor which triggering leads to robust type I IFN response via IRF3 and NFkB.
source: STING was originally identified as a cytosolic nucleic-acid sensor, which triggering leads to the induction of a robust type I IFN response via IRF3 and NFkB, and a rapid antiviral state that enables the control of viral infections (Zhong et al., 2008; Ishikawa and Barber, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Zhong et al., 2008 and Ishikawa and Barber, 2008.

claim: pDCs can secrete type I IFN independently of type I IFN signaling during VSV and MCMV infections.

claim: CD169+ MPs play a key role in regulating pDC activation in vivo.

evidence: This is concluded from all the experimental data showing CD169+ MPs are required for pDC activation.

claim: Further investigations are needed to determine the nature of STING-dependent signals from CD169+ MP that allow pDCs to achieve type I IFN-producing capacity and egress the BM.
